note.question: Will rival cloud providers voluntarily make multicloud deployment compatible, and when do compatibility mandates or cost-sharing policies help providers, buyers, and users?
note.overview: Two cloud providers strategically choose compatibility and prices while buyers choose single-cloud or multicloud allocation and end users choose adoption. The paper explicitly solves a four-stage subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium by backward induction.

coverage.note: The existing independently audited model map was decomposed into Mini-style components and linked back to the page-preserving source extraction.

models.name: Is Multicloud the Future? Desirability of Compatibility in Cloud Computing Market model
models.summary: Two cloud providers strategically choose compatibility and prices while buyers choose single-cloud or multicloud allocation and end users choose adoption. The paper explicitly solves a four-stage subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium by backward induction.
inputs: Provider locations, costs, buyer type distribution, latency technology, and adoption primitives are common knowledge
Buyers observe prices and compatibility regimes
End users know their own service valuation
decisions: Select a single-cloud or multicloud strategy
Adopt or reject the online service
assumptions: Two cloud providers each operate one data center in a different location and have enough capacity to serve all buyers
The baseline treats cloud resource provision as having zero marginal cost apart from compatibility cost

End users have heterogeneous service values, make adoption decisions over two periods, learn realized latency before period 2, and hold first-period beliefs that must be rational-expectations consistent
Compatibility is a unilateral, noncollaborative investment whose cost rises with demand served through the compatible platform
The baseline omits demand-driven latency, regional capacity constraints, and more than two providers

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: Stage 1: both providers simultaneously choose whether to offer compatibility. Stage 2: given those choices, providers simultaneously set cloud-resource prices. Stage 3: buyers choose provider A, provider B, or multicloud and allocate workloads if multicloud. Stage 4: end users decide whether to adopt the buyer's service.

components.label: Subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium with rational-expectations adoption
components.explanation: The model's equilibrium concept is Subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium with rational-expectations adoption. Section 4 states that the four-stage game is solved by backward induction to obtain the subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium. The analysis solves end-user adoption, buyer cloud choice and workload allocation, provider price competition, and finally the compatibility decisions for four possible Stage-1 regimes.
